messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajan Patel, a 41-year-old architect, came to treatment months after the end of a violent relationship that had left him feeling as if danger still lived inside his body. He described the abuse as unpredictable and disorienting rather than a single assault. His partner would drink heavily in the evening, and arguments would turn suddenly physical. Rajan remembered one night with particular clarity: the sharp smell of alcohol on her breath, her voice rising into rapid, half-coherent speech that he could not fully follow, and then the sickening lurch in his stomach just before she struck him. What stayed with him was not a smooth story but a handful of fixed images: the kitchen light reflecting off the counter, her face very close to his, his own hand against the wall. When he recalled it now, he did not feel as though he was remembering from a distance; the same terror arrived immediately, as if he were looking at photographs taken in the worst seconds of his life.

Since then, ordinary moments have become loaded with danger. If he feels physically unwell—nauseated, lightheaded, run down—his body reacts before he has time to think, because the sensation resembles the bodily warning he remembers from those nights. In the office, when contractors and clients overlap in a conference room and the conversation becomes incomprehensible chatter, he feels a jolt through his chest and shoulders before he can place why. Passing someone on the street or entering a restaurant where alcohol is on another person’s breath can have the same effect. In those moments he startles easily, scans the room, and feels a powerful need to stay alert, as though letting his guard down would be a mistake. The triggers do not just set off alarm; they also pull up the old images instantly. A whiff of whiskey or a blur of overlapping voices can bring back those snapshot scenes so vividly that he is again in the kitchen, flooded with the same terror.

Those moments also strike at how he has come to see himself. When a trigger hits, Rajan does not only feel afraid; he thinks, with painful certainty, that he should have seen it coming, should have known what to do, should have protected himself better. The smell of alcohol or the feeling of being physically off is enough to revive his sense that he cannot trust his own judgment. He had once understood himself as steady, competent, the person who could assess a situation and make sound decisions. Now he has come to believe he failed in a central role in life: to choose wisely, to keep himself and his marriage safe. Underneath that is a raw sense of betrayal by someone he trusted, and each trigger seems to prove that he was foolish to have trusted at all.

The memories deepen these beliefs. Because what returns are not softened narratives but stark mental photographs, Rajan feels confronted again and again with evidence of helplessness. He does not remember a sequence with perspective; he sees isolated moments and feels the terror in his body as if no time has passed. Looking at those internal snapshots, he concludes that he froze, that he did not do the right thing, that some essential instinct failed him. The more vividly he remembers being hurt by a person he loved, the more fixed his belief becomes that trust is dangerous and that he was betrayed in a way he should have prevented.

Over time this has tightened into a self-reinforcing pattern. Because Rajan doubts himself and feels he failed, he stays on guard constantly, convinced he cannot rely on his own judgment unless he remains hyperalert. Nights are the worst. He has difficulty falling asleep because he feels he needs to stay vigilant, as though sleep itself would leave him exposed. That chronic alertness leaves him jumpy during the day, and in that keyed-up state he notices possible danger everywhere: the stale smell of liquor in an elevator, the confusion of voices at a construction site, the bodily discomfort that comes with missed meals during long project deadlines. His threat system seems to teach him what to watch for, and the more he watches, the more often he is caught by those cues. Each alarm reaction primes the same visual fragments to burst forward; each burst of memory confirms that he is not safe and cannot trust himself. At work he has started avoiding crowded site meetings and asks younger associates to handle client dinners where alcohol will be served, a change that has begun to affect how visible he is in the firm. At home, his wife has noticed that he checks locks repeatedly and lies awake listening for sounds in the building.

What finally brought Rajan in was a recent incident at the office when a colleague, speaking over others in a noisy review meeting, moved close enough that Rajan caught the smell of beer from lunch. His body lurched into panic before he understood why, and for a moment all he could see were those frozen images from the kitchen. He left abruptly and sat in his car shaken and ashamed, thinking that even now he could not trust himself to manage a normal day. He is seeking help because he is frightened that his world is narrowing around vigilance and humiliation, and because he wants, more than anything, to stop feeling that the worst moments of that relationship are still happening inside him.
